title: Data Center Server Rack
subtitle: Eight 2U servers, redundant power and a cooling unit in one sealed cabinet
summary: A server rack is a building inside a building. The frame holds standard 19-inch equipment, the door and side panels control airflow, and the top-of-rack switch ties every server to the network. Power comes in on two independent buses, and a precision cooling unit removes the heat that the servers turn electricity into.

parts.name: Base Plinth
parts.short: Levels the rack and spreads its load
parts.detail: The plinth carries the cabinet's feet and spreads several hundred kilograms over the raised floor.

parts.name: Rack Frame
parts.detail: Four posts and horizontal rails form the EIA-310 rack. The U markings set where each server sits.

parts.name: Side Panels
parts.short: Close the sides of the cabinet
parts.detail: Side panels keep cold air in front of the servers and hot air behind them.

parts.name: Top Panel
parts.short: Caps the rack and carries cable entry
parts.detail: The top panel closes the cabinet and provides brush strips for cables leaving the rack.

parts.name: Front Door
parts.short: Lets air in and lets engineers see the LEDs
parts.detail: A perforated or glazed door protects the equipment while allowing cool air to reach the server intakes.

parts.name: Server Units
parts.detail: Each server has its own CPUs, memory, drives and fans. The front panel carries drive bays and status LEDs.

parts.name: Top-of-Rack Switches
parts.short: Connect every server to the network
parts.detail: Two switches give redundant uplinks. Each server connects to both, so one switch can fail without dropping traffic.

parts.name: Patch Panel
parts.detail: Ports on the patch panel connect the rack to the building's fiber and copper backbone.

parts.name: Cable Management
parts.detail: Vertical rings and a rear tray keep cables tidy and leave a clear path for exhaust air.

parts.name: Power Distribution
parts.detail: Each server has redundant supplies connected to separate PDUs, so a single feed can be serviced safely.

parts.name: Server Fans
parts.short: Pull cold air through each chassis
parts.detail: Hot-swappable fans move air from the front intakes across the CPUs and out the rear.

parts.name: UPS
parts.short: Bridges the gap to generator power
parts.detail: The uninterruptible supply carries the rack through short outages and conditions the incoming power.

parts.name: Cooling Unit
parts.short: Removes the heat the servers produce
parts.detail: A precision air conditioner blows cold air into the aisle and takes hot air back. Almost all the electrical power ends up as heat.

parts.name: Monitoring Panel
parts.detail: The panel displays rack inlet temperature, power draw and any active alarm.

parts.name: Nameplate
parts.detail: The plate records the rack number, power capacity and owner.

steps.title: A standard width makes everything fit
steps.body: The 19-inch rack and its U height are shared across vendors. Any 2U server slides onto the same rails, which is why data centres can mix equipment from many makers.

steps.title: Cold in the front, hot out the back
steps.body: Servers pull cool air through their front intakes and exhaust it behind the rack. Doors, panels and blanking plates keep the two air streams from mixing.

steps.title: Two paths for every packet
steps.body: Each server connects to two top-of-rack switches, and the switches uplink over separate paths. A cable or switch failure reroutes traffic without stopping the service.

steps.title: Power and heat are the real limits
steps.body: A rack is limited by how much power it can draw and how much heat the room can remove. Redundant PDUs and a dedicated cooling unit keep both within safe limits.

quiz.prompt: Tap the switches that connect the servers to the network.
Tap the unit that removes heat from the rack.
Tap the part that supplies power during a short outage.
Why does each server connect to two switches?
choices: So one switch can fail without losing the network
quiz.explain: Redundant links let traffic fail over to the second switch.

quiz.prompt: Where does almost all the electricity used by a server end up?
quiz.explain: Computing converts nearly all its electrical energy into heat, which the cooling system must remove.
